medium.titulo: AI Engineer Became a Thing in 2026 And It Happened Faster Than I Expected
medium.resumo: From Software Engineer to AI Engineer: How the tech job market changed in less than a year.
medium.conteudo_html:
From Software Engineer to AI Engineer: How the tech job market changed in less than a year.

I remember searching for jobs back in 2025.

Most of the job titles I came across were familiar: Software Engineer, QA Engineer, Backend Developer, Frontend Developer, and Full Stack Developer.

That was the landscape I was used to.

But now, in November 2026, something feels completely different.

I open LinkedIn, browse job boards, and look at company career pages. Suddenly, I see AI Engineer, Generative AI Engineer, Agentic AI Developer, AI Application Developer, and AI/ML Engineer everywhere.

And honestly, it makes me stop and think.

How did the industry change this much in less than a year?

A 12-Month Shift That Changed Everything

In 2025, AI was already a major topic in technology. We had ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Claude, and many other AI tools.

But for many software engineers, AI was still something we integrated into applications or used to improve productivity.

Fast forward to November 2026.

AI is no longer just a feature in a software application. It has become the foundation of entire products, development workflows, and business strategies.

Companies aren’t simply looking for developers who can build APIs, websites, and backend systems anymore.

They increasingly want engineers who can build intelligent systems.

And that has created an entirely new wave of job titles.

From Software Engineers to AI Engineers

One of the most interesting things I’ve noticed is how the definition of an engineer seems to be expanding.

Traditional software engineering skills are still important. We still need APIs, databases, authentication, distributed systems, testing, deployment, and reliable infrastructure.

But now, another layer is becoming increasingly valuable.

Engineers are expected to understand:

  • Large Language Models (LLMs)
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
  • AI agents and agentic workflows
  • Vector databases and semantic search
  • AI model integration and orchestration
  • Evaluation, monitoring, and AI reliability

The interesting part?

Many of these systems are still built using the same engineering principles we already know.

The difference is that we’re now building applications that can reason, retrieve information, generate responses, and execute actions.

AI engineering isn’t replacing software engineering. It’s expanding what software engineering can do.

The Rise of Agentic AI Developers

Another job title that caught my attention is Agentic AI Developer.

A few years ago, building an application usually meant writing code that followed predefined logic.

Now, we’re seeing systems where AI agents can:

  • Understand user requests.
  • Decide which tools to use.
  • Retrieve information from different sources.
  • Execute multi-step workflows.
  • Collaborate with other agents.
  • Complete tasks with limited human intervention.

Frameworks such as LangChain, LangGraph, and other agent orchestration tools have become part of the conversation.

This changes how we think about application development.

We’re no longer just designing functions and endpoints. We’re also designing workflows, tools, context, memory, and decision-making processes for AI systems.

That’s a fascinating shift for anyone working in software engineering.

Why Did This Happen So Quickly?

I think several things happened at the same time.

1. AI became useful in real products

Businesses moved beyond experimenting with chatbots and started looking for practical ways to automate workflows, improve customer experiences, and reduce repetitive work.

2. AI development tools became more accessible

Developers can now build AI-powered applications using APIs, frameworks, and managed infrastructure without training large models from scratch.

3. Businesses started thinking differently about software

Instead of asking only, “Can we build an application for this process?”, companies increasingly ask, “Can AI make this process intelligent or automated?”

4. The demand for AI integration created new engineering opportunities

Organizations need people who understand both software engineering and AI capabilities. That combination is becoming increasingly valuable.

What Does This Mean for Software Engineers?

For me, this is probably the most important question.

If you’re already a software engineer, should you completely change your career direction?

I don’t think so.

Instead, I think the opportunity is to build on what you already know.

Backend engineers can learn LLM integration, RAG pipelines, and AI orchestration.

Full-stack developers can build AI-powered products and intelligent user experiences.

QA engineers can explore AI evaluation, automated testing, and quality assurance for AI systems.

Data analysts can expand into data engineering, machine learning, and AI-powered analytics.

The foundation is still engineering.

But the opportunities are expanding.

The Part That Makes Me Think

What surprises me most isn’t simply the number of AI-related job titles.

It’s the speed.

In less than a year, the conversations around software careers have changed significantly.

In 2025, I was mainly searching for Software Engineer and Developer positions.

In November 2026, I’m seeing opportunities that didn’t appear nearly as frequently in my job searches before.

AI Engineer.

Agentic AI Developer.

GenAI Application Engineer.

AI-Native Software Engineer.

And it makes me wonder what the job market will look like by the end of 2027.

Will AI engineering become a standard expectation for software engineers?

Will agentic systems become a normal part of enterprise applications?

Will today’s AI-specific job titles eventually become as common as Backend Developer or Full Stack Engineer?

I don’t know the answers yet.

But one thing feels certain.

The technology industry isn’t waiting for anyone to catch up.

Final Thoughts

I still believe strong software engineering fundamentals matter more than ever.

Understanding architecture, writing maintainable code, designing APIs, working with databases, debugging production systems, and building reliable applications are skills that don’t suddenly disappear because AI becomes more powerful.

However, the engineers who combine those fundamentals with AI capabilities may find themselves in an increasingly interesting position.

For me, this shift is not just about learning another framework or adding another technology to a CV.

It’s about understanding how the way we build software is changing.

And perhaps the most important skill in this new era isn’t mastering one particular AI framework.

It’s the ability to keep learning while the industry changes around you.

Because if the last 12 months have taught me anything, it’s this:

The future of software engineering might look very different from what we imagined in 2025.

And we’re already living in it.

What do you think? Will AI Engineering become the new standard for software developers, or will it remain a specialized career path?

medium.titulo: Not Every Rule Belongs in CLAUDE.md: When a Script or Hook Is Better
medium.resumo: You have a line in your CLAUDE.md that says "Never edit existing migrations." Claude Code follows it. Almost always. Then one afternoon it…
medium.conteudo_html:
You have a line in your CLAUDE.md that says "Never edit existing migrations." Claude Code follows it. Almost always. Then one afternoon it "fixes" a column type directly in 0007_add_orders.sql, and you spend an hour untangling a database that no longer matches its history.

The usual reaction is to make the line louder. Anthropic’s Claude Code best practices say adding IMPORTANT probably won’t fix it: either the file is long enough that the line gets lost, or it’s a rule that can’t have exceptions, and that kind of rule belongs in a hook.

In an earlier article I covered what to cut from a long CLAUDE.md. This one is about the lines worth keeping that still fail you: should each one stay a sentence, become a script, or become a hook?

Why a sentence can’t guarantee anything

The memory docs are direct about this: Claude treats CLAUDE.md files "as context, not enforced configuration." The best-practices page splits every instruction into two kinds:

  • Non-deterministic. You write it, the model reads it and decides what to do. Your prompt, CLAUDE.md and skills are in this group. Claude usually follows them, but there's no guarantee.
  • Deterministic. You configure it, and Claude Code (the harness) applies it every time. Hooks, deny rules and managed settings are in this group.

The same page says that most of the time you want Claude to decide, because almost every guideline has exceptions. So the goal isn’t to turn your file into hooks. It’s to find the few rules where “almost always” isn’t good enough.

The three-way test

For each line in your CLAUDE.md, ask three questions in order.

1. Does it have exceptions? “Prefer named exports”, “use the error helpers in src/lib/errors.ts". These are guidelines, and you want Claude to use judgment. Keep them in CLAUDE.md. The best-practices page uses "Prefer named exports" as its example of a rule that should not become a hook.

2. Is it a procedure with exact steps? “Before committing, run the linter, then the type checker, then the unit tests, and if the API changed, regenerate the client.” That’s a sequence of commands written as prose. Claude has to read it, remember it and type it correctly every time. Turn it into a script, and leave one line in CLAUDE.md that names the script.

3. Must it always (or never) happen, with zero exceptions? “Never edit an existing migration.” “Never touch .env." "Don't finish until the type check passes." If a single miss costs you real time, make it a hook, so the outcome no longer depends on what the model remembers.

A handy signal from the docs: if you keep adding emphasis to a CLAUDE.md line and Claude still misses it, that line is a candidate for a hook. And the reverse: if you have hooks for things that are only preferences, delete them and let Claude decide.

Step 1: Turn procedures into a script

Here’s the kind of block that grows in a CLAUDE.md over time:

## Before you finish
- Run `pnpm lint`
- Then run `pnpm tsc --noEmit`
- Then run `pnpm test --run`
- If you changed anything in src/api, run `pnpm gen:client` first
- Fix every error before saying you're done

Move the commands into a file the whole team can run:

#!/bin/bash
# scripts/check.sh: the one command that says "this change is ready"
set -e
pnpm lint
pnpm tsc --noEmit
pnpm test --run

And replace the block with a single line:

- Run `./scripts/check.sh` before you say a change is done.

(The commands are an example for a pnpm/TypeScript project. Use whatever your project actually runs.)

The line costs less context in every session, the steps can’t drift because there’s one copy and it’s code, and the same script works for you, for CI and, in a moment, for a hook. The best-practices page puts it this way: if your repo already has a check like this, the single most useful line in your CLAUDE.md is the command that runs it.

Step 2: Turn “never” rules into a PreToolUse hook

A PreToolUse hook runs before a tool call and can block it. According to the hooks guide, Claude Code passes the tool call as JSON on the script's stdin. If the script exits with code 2, the call is blocked and whatever it wrote to stderr goes back to Claude as feedback, so it can adjust. Exit code 0 means no objection, and the normal permission flow applies.

The guide includes an example that blocks edits to protected files such as .env. Here's a variation for the migrations rule. It blocks edits to migration files that already exist, but still lets Claude create a new one, because "add a new migration" is exactly what you want it to do instead:

#!/bin/bash
# .claude/hooks/protect-migrations.sh
# Block edits to migration files that already exist. New migrations are allowed.
INPUT=$(cat)
FILE_PATH=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty')

if [[ "$FILE_PATH" == *migrations/* && -e "$FILE_PATH" ]]; then
  echo "Blocked: $FILE_PATH is an existing migration. Add a new migration file instead of editing this one." >&2
  exit 2
fi

exit 0

Make it executable (chmod +x .claude/hooks/protect-migrations.sh) and register it in .claude/settings.json, using the same structure as the guide's example:

{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/protect-migrations.sh"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Test the script before you trust it

You don’t need a Claude Code session to check the logic. Feed the script the same kind of JSON it will receive and look at the exit code. I did this in a small throwaway project at /tmp/shop with one existing migration, then simulated three tool calls:

for call in "Edit migrations/0007_add_orders.sql" "Write migrations/0008_add_refunds.sql" "Edit src/service.ts"; do
  set -- $call
  echo "--- $1 $2"
  echo "{\"hook_event_name\":\"PreToolUse\",\"tool_name\":\"$1\",\"tool_input\":{\"file_path\":\"$PWD/$2\"}}" | ./.claude/hooks/protect-migrations.sh
  echo "exit code: $?"
done

Output:

--- Edit migrations/0007_add_orders.sql
Blocked: /tmp/shop/migrations/0007_add_orders.sql is an existing migration. Add a new migration file instead of editing this one.
exit code: 2
--- Write migrations/0008_add_refunds.sql
exit code: 0
--- Edit src/service.ts
exit code: 0

The existing migration is blocked with a message Claude can act on; the new migration and the source file go through. This tests the script, not Claude Code itself. Inside a session, the guide suggests running /hooks to confirm the hook is registered, then asking Claude to make the edit you want blocked.

One gap to know about

A hook that matches Edit|Write only sees those tools. The hooks guide points out that Claude can also change files by running shell commands, so a sed -i through the Bash tool wouldn't pass through this script. If you need to catch every change, the guide suggests also matching Bash and checking modified files with git status --porcelain, or adding a Stop hook that scans the working tree once per turn.

Step 3: Turn “don’t finish until” into a Stop hook

A Stop hook runs whenever Claude tries to end its turn. If the hook exits with code 2, Claude is sent back to work, and the stderr output becomes the reason. The best-practices page shows this with a type check:

{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "pnpm tsc --noEmit 1>&2 || exit 2" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Since you already have scripts/check.sh, you can point the hook at it instead, so the rule lives in one place: "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/scripts/check.sh 1>&2 || exit 2". The 1>&2 matters, because it sends the tool output to stderr, where Claude will read it.

Two things to know before you add one. Stop hooks fire whenever Claude finishes responding, not only when a task is complete, so a slow check runs often. And there’s a safety cap: per the docs, if the hook blocks eight stops in a row with no tool call in between, Claude Code overrides the next block and ends the turn. A check that can never pass won’t trap you in a loop, but it also won’t get fixed by itself.

What stays in CLAUDE.md

What’s left should be things Claude can’t see in the code: commands, conventions that need judgment, gotchas. One line per script, not one per step, and no rule written twice, once as a sentence and once as a hook. Don’t overcorrect, either: the docs describe a hook as a tool for a rule with zero exceptions. And hooks are code that runs on your machine, so review them like any script, especially in a repo you didn’t write.

A 10-minute checklist

  • Read every line in your CLAUDE.md and tag it: guideline, procedure or never/always rule.
  • Move each multi-step procedure into a script and replace it with one line that names the script.
  • Pick the one or two never/always rules where a single miss really hurts.
  • Write a PreToolUse hook for "never" rules and a Stop hook for "don't finish until" rules.
  • Test each hook script by piping sample JSON into it and checking the exit code.
  • Run /hooks in Claude Code to confirm the hook is registered.
  • Delete the sentence version of any rule a hook now enforces.

Where to go next

If you want the short version of what belongs in the file, the free CLAUDE.md Quick-Start Cheat Sheet covers what to include, what to cut, the one-line test for every line, and a map of the configuration stack beyond CLAUDE.md (slash commands, subagents, hooks, skills and plugins) with a simple framework for when to reach for each, in six pages.

When you’re ready to build the whole stack, CLAUDE.md: The Complete Claude Code Configuration Guide has chapters on hooks, subagents, skills, plugins, security and team governance, plus three real-world configuration walkthroughs, the nine most common mistakes and a 30-day plan to build your setup from scratch.

This article was written with the assistance of AI and reviewed by the author. Claude Code behavior is described from Anthropic’s official documentation (hooks guide, memory and best-practices pages). The hook script is the author’s adaptation of the docs’ protected-files example; the output shown is its real output when fed sample JSON in a throwaway project, not output from a Claude Code session. The CLAUDE.md block and check.sh are illustrative examples. PromptMaster guides are independent and not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

medium.titulo: How to Use Claude AI to Save Time: 5 Practical Tips
medium.resumo: Most of us don’t have a time problem. Our days get eaten by small tasks.
medium.conteudo_html:
Most of us don’t have a time problem. Our days get eaten by small tasks. A long email needs a careful reply. A report has to be read before a meeting. A document is full of mistakes you can no longer spot. None of these tasks is hard, but together they take hours.

I first realized how useful Claude can be during a very busy period of my life. I was doing a government internship, and at the same time my university announced mid-term exams. I had limited time and no clear idea how to start preparing. Instead of wasting days feeling stuck, I asked Claude for practical tips on organizing my preparation. I followed them step by step, and when the results came, I had earned a very good grade. That experience showed me that Claude is not just a tool for answering questions. It can help you start when you feel overwhelmed.

An AI assistant like Claude can take over the slow parts of this work. It can read documents, organize information, prepare drafts, and handle repetitive jobs. You still make the decisions. You just don’t begin every task from zero. This guide covers five practical ways to use Claude AI to save time. Each tip has an example prompt you can copy and try today. No technical experience is needed.

What Is Claude AI and How Can It Save Time?

Claude is an AI assistant developed by Anthropic. You type questions or instructions in everyday language, and it replies in text. Depending on your plan and the features available, you can also upload supported files and ask Claude to work with them. It saves time because so much daily work is really reading, writing, and organizing information, and those are things Claude does well. A first draft that takes you an hour can appear in a minute or two. Your time then goes into checking and improving it. Claude isn’t perfect, though. It can misunderstand an instruction, state a wrong fact confidently, or give outdated information. Think of it as a fast assistant whose work you always review. Check important names, dates, numbers, and claims yourself.

Tip 1: Summarize Long Documents in Minutes

Reports, research papers, business documents, and long email threads often hide a few useful points inside pages of detail. Reading everything carefully takes hours, and skipping it is risky. Claude can help you find what matters faster. Upload a supported document or paste the text, then say exactly what you need. A vague request gets a vague summary.

Try this prompt:

I’ve attached a report. Summarize it in 8 bullet points. List important deadlines, numbers, and action items separately. At the end, tell me which two sections I should read in full.

The last line is the useful part. It doesn’t only shorten the document, it also tells you where to spend your attention.

How to Get Better Document Summaries

  • Explain your purpose. Tell Claude whether you’re reading for work, study, or general understanding.
  • Choose a format. Ask for bullet points, a short paragraph, or a table.
  • Ask follow-up questions. If one section is unclear, ask Claude to explain just that part.
  • Look for gaps. Ask what important questions the document leaves unanswered.

One caution: treat a summary as a map, not the full territory. For legal, financial, or medical documents, read the important parts yourself before you act on them.

Tip 2: Draft and Edit Writing Faster

The blank page wastes more time than most people admit. You know what you want to say, but the first sentence refuses to arrive. Claude removes that problem by giving you something to react to, and editing a draft is much faster than creating one.

This works for emails, application letters, social media posts, blog outlines, and everyday messages.

Try this prompt for an email:

Write a polite but firm email to a client who is two weeks late on payment. Keep it under 120 words. Don’t sound angry, and include a clear deadline of Friday.

You’ll get a usable draft in seconds. Don’t send it unchanged, though. Read it, adjust it, and make sure it sounds like you.

How to Make AI Writing Sound Like You

AI drafts can feel formal or stiff. A few habits fix this:

  1. Share a sample of your own writing. Paste an email you wrote and ask Claude to match the tone. This is the best trick for a natural voice.
  2. Give simple instructions. Ask for plain English, short sentences, and no buzzwords.
  3. Edit the result. Change a few phrases, add a personal detail, and delete anything you wouldn’t say out loud.

Use Claude as an Editor

If you’d rather write everything yourself, Claude can still save you time as a proofreader. Try:

Proofread the following text for grammar and spelling only. Don’t change my wording, meaning, or style. Show me the corrections.

For deeper feedback, try this:

Read this article and point out sentences that feel repetitive, unclear, or unnecessary. Don’t rewrite anything. Just explain what needs improvement.

Your writing stays yours, and you catch problems you can no longer see after reading your own text too many times.

Tip 3: Use Claude as a Research Partner

Research usually means opening many tabs, reading the same idea in different words, and losing an hour. Claude can’t replace careful research, but it makes the early stage much quicker. It can explain an unfamiliar topic, organize your ideas, and suggest what to look into next.

Try this prompt:

I’m new to the topic of solar panel prices for homes. Explain the basics in simple English. Then give me 10 questions I should ask before requesting a price quote.

The second half matters most. A good list of questions often separates a confused beginner from an informed buyer.

Useful Ways to Research with Claude

  • Learn the basics first. Ask for a beginner explanation, then go deeper step by step.
  • Compare options. Give Claude details about three products and ask for a comparison table.
  • See both sides. Ask for the strongest arguments for and against an idea.
  • Plan a report. Request a list of subtopics and the types of sources to look for.
  • Understand hard concepts. Ask for an explanation using an everyday example, and keep asking “why?” until it makes sense.

Always Verify Important Information

This is where people get into trouble. Claude can give wrong statistics, dates, quotations, or sources, and it can sound completely sure while doing it. Information about recent events may also be outdated. Use Claude to understand a topic and plan your research. For any fact you’ll publish or act on, go to the original research, official reports, or other reliable sources.

You can also ask Claude to help with this:

Which parts of your answer need fact-checking? Identify specific claims and suggest how I can verify them using reliable sources.

When I was preparing for my mid-terms, my biggest problem was not a lack of effort. It was not knowing where to begin. I asked Claude to explain how to plan my exam preparation while managing an internship. It gave me a simple starting point, and I built my own schedule from it. I still checked every detail against my course material, because the plan was only useful once it matched what my teachers actually expected.

Tip 4: Write Better Prompts to Get Better Answers

What you get from Claude depends heavily on what you ask. If you only type “write about time management,” Claude knows almost nothing about your needs and will give a general answer. Then you waste ten minutes going back and forth. Learning to write clear prompts may be the biggest time-saver on this list, because it improves everything else.

A Simple Formula for Better Prompts

A good prompt usually includes four things:

  1. Context: your situation and background.
  2. Task: exactly what you want done.
  3. Format: a list, table, email, or paragraph.
  4. Limits: length, tone, and things to avoid.

Weak prompt:

Write about time management.

Better prompt:

I’m a university student with three hours of free time each evening. Create a realistic weekly study plan using a table. Include no more than two main tasks per day and leave time for breaks.

The second prompt takes thirty extra seconds to write and can save you five rounds of corrections.

More Habits That Help

  • Give an example. If you want a certain style, show a sample.
  • Let Claude ask first. Say, “Before you start, ask me any questions you need,” so it doesn’t have to guess.
  • Split big tasks. Request an outline, approve it, then build the piece section by section.
  • Say what went wrong. “Too formal, and the second point isn’t relevant” works far better than “try again.”
  • Stay in one conversation. Claude can use what you said earlier in the same chat, so you don’t repeat the background.

If you do the same kind of task often, save your best prompts in a notes app and reuse them.

Tip 5: Handle Repetitive Tasks More Efficiently

Every job has small tasks that come back again and again: formatting information, writing similar messages, making checklists, cleaning up notes. These are a good fit for Claude.

Turn Messy Information Into Organized Data

Say you’ve copied names and contact details from several documents, and they’re all in different formats. Try:

Here’s a list of contacts in different formats. Organize it into a table with columns for name, phone number, and city. Highlight any missing information.

Create Reusable Templates

If you send similar emails often, build a template once:

Create a reusable email template for following up after a job interview. Add placeholders in brackets for personal details. Provide one formal version and one friendly version.

Prepare Checklists and Plans

Planning an event involves many small responsibilities. A checklist gives you a structure to adjust:

I’m organizing a workshop for 40 people. Create a checklist of everything I need to prepare, divided into two weeks before, one week before, and the event day.

Get Help With Spreadsheets

You don’t need to memorize Excel formulas. Describe what you want in plain words:

In Excel, I have dates in column A and amounts in column B. Give me a formula that adds only the amounts from the current month. Explain how the formula works.

Test any formula on sample data before using it in an important spreadsheet.

Organize Meeting Notes

Paste your rough notes and ask:

Turn these notes into a clear meeting summary. Separate the main discussion points, decisions, and next steps. Use bullet points.

Should You Use the Free Plan or a Paid Plan?

If you’re just starting, the free option is enough to try every tip in this article. Free access usually comes with usage limits, so you may have to wait if you use it heavily. Paid plans generally offer higher limits and extra features. They make sense if you use Claude daily for work, or if you keep hitting the limits. Plans and prices change, so check the official Claude website for current details before deciding. A sensible approach is to start free for a week or two, notice which tasks you actually use it for, and upgrade only if the limits get in your way.

Common Mistakes That Waste Time Instead of Saving It

Using AI badly can create extra work. Avoid these mistakes:

  • Trusting every answer. One wrong fact in a client email or published article can cost more than the time you saved.
  • Sharing private information. Don’t enter passwords, banking details, or confidential personal or business data. Remove names and identifying details when possible.
  • Copying without reading. Read everything before you send or publish it. Readers notice generic or incorrect text.
  • Writing unclear prompts. Specific instructions get better results than hoping Claude guesses what you mean.
  • Using AI for everything. If explaining a task takes longer than doing it, just do it yourself.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Claude AI free to use?

Claude offers a free option with usage limits, as well as paid plans with more access and features. Availability, pricing, and limits can change, so check the official Claude website for current information.

Can I use Claude AI for work and business?

Yes. Many people use it for emails, summaries, planning, and organizing information. Review the output carefully and follow your workplace’s rules about sharing confidential information.

Can Claude AI replace my job?

Claude can handle some routine tasks, but it doesn’t replace human judgment, responsibility, creativity, or personal relationships. How AI affects a job depends on the kind of work and how the tools are used.

Is Claude AI always accurate?

No. It can misunderstand questions, produce incorrect facts, or give outdated information. Verify important details with reliable sources before making decisions.

Do I need technical skills to use Claude?

No. You can write to Claude in everyday language. Clear instructions and a useful example are usually enough to get started.

What is the best way to start?

Pick one simple task, such as summarizing a document or drafting an email. Practice giving clear instructions, check the result, and then move on to more complicated work.

Final Thoughts

You don’t need to use all five tips at once. Start with the task that eats the most time in your week.

If long documents slow you down, ask Claude for a summary. If emails take too long, let it prepare the first draft. If you keep organizing the same kind of information, build a template once and reuse it. What matters is finding the places where Claude really helps you.

Quick recap:

  1. Summarize long documents so you read only what matters.
  2. Draft and edit without starting from a blank page.
  3. Use Claude for research to understand topics, then verify the facts.
  4. Write better prompts with context, task, format, and limits.
  5. Handle repetitive tasks with templates, checklists, and organized data.

Claude isn’t a replacement for your own thinking. It’s a tool that clears away routine work so you have more time for things that need your attention. Start with one tip, try it this week, and see whether it genuinely saves you time.

medium.titulo: Vue.js Fundamentals Made Easy: A Beginner’s Guide to Building Modern Web Applications
medium.resumo: Modern web development is not just about writing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
medium.conteudo_html:
Modern web development is not just about writing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

Today’s applications need dynamic interfaces, reusable components, reactive data, and efficient ways to manage user interactions.

This is where Vue.js comes in.

Vue.js is a progressive JavaScript framework used to build user interfaces and single-page applications. It is beginner-friendly, flexible, and powerful enough for large-scale applications.

If you are starting with Vue.js or want to strengthen your JavaScript frontend fundamentals, this guide will help you understand the core concepts with practical examples.

Let’s get started!

1. What Is Vue.js?

Vue.js is an open-source JavaScript framework for building user interfaces.

It allows developers to create dynamic applications by connecting JavaScript data with HTML templates.

For example, imagine you have a counter application.

With plain JavaScript, you need to manually find an HTML element and update its content whenever the value changes.

With Vue.js, you simply connect the data to the template. When the data changes, Vue automatically updates the interface.

Why Do Developers Use Vue.js?

  • Easy to learn and understand.
  • Component-based architecture.
  • Reactive data management.
  • Reusable UI components.
  • Flexible integration with existing projects.
  • Excellent ecosystem for modern frontend development.

Vue is commonly used for dashboards, admin panels, e-commerce applications, SaaS platforms, and interactive web applications.

2. Understanding the Vue Project Structure

Before writing Vue code, let’s understand how a typical Vue 3 project is organized.

A common project structure looks like this:

my-vue-app/
│
├── public/
│
├── src/
│   ├── assets/
│   ├── components/
│   ├── views/
│   ├── router/
│   ├── App.vue
│   └── main.js
│
├── index.html
├── package.json
└── vite.config.js

Here is what these files and folders do:

  • components/ — Stores reusable Vue components.
  • views/ — Stores page-level components.
  • assets/ — Contains images, styles, and other assets.
  • router/ — Contains application routing configuration.
  • App.vue — The root Vue component.
  • main.js — The application entry point.
  • package.json — Manages project dependencies and scripts.

Vue applications commonly use Single File Components with the .vue extension.

3. Understanding Vue Single File Components (SFC)

A Vue Single File Component allows you to organize HTML, JavaScript, and CSS in one file.

Example:

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const message = ref('Hello Vue.js!')
</script>
<template>
    <h1>{{ message }}</h1>
</template>
<style scoped>
h1 {
    color: #42b883;
}
</style>

A Vue component usually contains three main sections:

Script: Handles JavaScript logic and data.

Template: Defines the HTML structure of the component.

Style: Contains component-specific CSS.

The scoped attribute ensures that the component's styles are scoped to that component.

The script setup syntax is a convenient way to write Composition API code in Vue 3.

4. Understanding Reactivity in Vue.js

Reactivity is one of the most important concepts in Vue.

It means that when application data changes, Vue automatically updates the relevant parts of the user interface.

Let’s understand this with an example.

Using ref()

The ref() function creates a reactive reference.

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
const increment = () => {
    count.value++
}
</script>
<template>
    <h2>Count: {{ count }}</h2>
    <button @click="increment">
        Increase
    </button>
</template>

Here:

  • ref(0) creates a reactive value.
  • count.value accesses or updates the value in JavaScript.
  • {{ count }} displays the value in the template.
  • @click listens for button clicks.

An interesting detail: inside JavaScript, you access a ref using .value. In Vue templates, top-level refs are automatically unwrapped.

Using reactive()

Vue also provides reactive() to create reactive objects.

<script setup>
import { reactive } from 'vue'

const user = reactive({
    name: 'Jalis',
    role: 'Developer',
    experience: 4
})
</script>
<template>
    <h2>{{ user.name }}</h2>
    <p>{{ user.role }}</p>
    <p>{{ user.experience }} Years Experience</p>
</template>

The main difference:

ref()reactive()Works with primitive values and objectsDesigned for objectsAccess value using .value in JavaScriptAccess properties directlyCan be reassigned as a referenceCannot be replaced as a whole while retaining the original reactive connection

Developer Tip: Use ref() for most reactive state, especially when you need to replace the value. Use reactive() when working with a reactive object.

5. Understanding Vue Directives

Directives are special Vue attributes that add reactive behavior to HTML elements.

Some important Vue directives include:

A. v-if

v-if conditionally renders an element.

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const isLoggedIn = ref(true)
</script>
<template>
    <h2 v-if="isLoggedIn">
        Welcome Back!
    </h2>
    <h2 v-else>
        Please Login
    </h2>
</template>

If isLoggedIn is true, the first heading appears.

Otherwise, Vue renders the second heading.

B. v-show

v-show controls an element's visibility using CSS.

<template>
    <h2 v-show="isLoggedIn">
        Welcome Back!
    </h2>
</template>

Unlike v-if, v-show keeps the element in the DOM and changes its CSS display property.

When should you use them?

  • Use v-if when a condition changes infrequently.
  • Use v-show when visibility changes frequently.

C. v-for

v-for is used to render lists.

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const users = ref([
    { id: 1, name: 'Jalis' },
    { id: 2, name: 'Rahim' },
    { id: 3, name: 'Karim' }
])
</script>
<template>
    <ul>
        <li v-for="user in users" :key="user.id">
            {{ user.name }}
        </li>
    </ul>
</template>

The :key attribute helps Vue identify individual elements when updating a list.

Always use a stable, unique key whenever possible.

D. v-bind

v-bind dynamically binds HTML attributes to JavaScript values.

<script setup>
const imageUrl = '/images/product.png'
</script

<template>
    <img :src="imageUrl" alt="Product">
</template>

The shorthand for v-bind is :.

E. v-model

v-model creates two-way data binding between form inputs and JavaScript state.

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const name = ref('')
</script>
<template>
    <input v-model="name" placeholder="Enter your name">
    <p>Hello, {{ name }}</p>
</template>

When the user types something, the reactive variable updates automatically.

6. Handling Events in Vue.js

Applications need to respond to user interactions.

For example:

  • Button clicks
  • Form submissions
  • Input changes
  • Mouse events
  • Keyboard events

Vue provides the v-on directive to handle events.

The shorthand is @.

Example:

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

Here, clicking the button executes the showMessage() function.

You can also use event modifiers:

<form @submit.prevent="submitForm">
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

const message = ref('')
const showMessage = () => {
    message.value = 'Button clicked successfully!'
}
</script>
<template>
    <button @click="showMessage">
        Click Me
    </button>
    <p>{{ message }}</p>
</template>

The .prevent modifier prevents the browser's default form submission behavior.

7. Understanding Computed Properties

Computed properties are useful when you need to calculate values based on reactive data.

Let’s imagine you have a product price and quantity.

Instead of calculating the total price repeatedly in your template, you can use computed().

<script setup>
import { ref, computed } from 'vue'

const price = ref(100)
const quantity = ref(3)
const totalPrice = computed(() => {
    return price.value * quantity.value
})
</script>
<template>
    <h2>Price: {{ price }}</h2>
    <h2>Quantity: {{ quantity }}</h2>
    <h2>Total: {{ totalPrice }}</h2>
</template>

Whenever the price or quantity changes, Vue recalculates the computed value when needed.

Computed vs Methods

ComputedMethodsCached based on reactive dependenciesRuns whenever calledUseful for derived valuesUseful for actions and operationsRecalculates when dependencies changeExecutes on each invocation

Use computed properties for values derived from existing state.

8. Understanding Watchers

Sometimes you need to perform an action when a reactive value changes.

For this purpose, Vue provides watch().

Example:

<script setup>
import { ref, watch } from 'vue'

const search = ref('')
watch(search, (newValue, oldValue) => {
    console.log('New Search:', newValue)
    console.log('Previous Search:', oldValue)
})
</script>
<template>
    <input v-model="search" placeholder="Search products">
</template>

Whenever the search value changes, the watcher executes.

When Should You Use watch()?

  • Watching search input changes.
  • Calling an API after a filter changes.
  • Saving data when a setting changes.
  • Performing side effects based on reactive state.

Remember: Computed is generally for calculating values. Watch is for responding to changes with side effects.

9. Understanding Components in Vue.js

Components are reusable building blocks of Vue applications.

Imagine you are building an e-commerce website.

You might have:

  • Navbar
  • Product Card
  • Product List
  • Shopping Cart
  • Footer
  • Checkout Form

Instead of writing everything inside one large Vue file, you can create separate components.

Example:

ProductCard.vue

<script setup>
defineProps({
    name: String,
    price: Number
})
</script?

<template>
    <div class="product-card">
        <h3>{{ name }}</h3>
        <p>Price: {{ price }}</p>
    </div>
</template>

Now you can reuse this component multiple times.

<script setup>
import ProductCard from './components/ProductCard.vue'
</script>

<template>
    <ProductCard
        name="Keyboard"
        :price="1500"
    />
    <ProductCard
        name="Mouse"
        :price="800"
    />
</template>

This makes your application easier to maintain and scale.

10. Understanding Props and Emits

Props and Emits are important concepts in component communication.

A. Props

Props allow a parent component to pass data to a child component.

For example:

<ProductCard
    name="Keyboard"
    :price="1500"
/>

The child component receives these values through defineProps().

Props should be treated as read-only inside the child component.

B. Emits

Emits allow a child component to communicate with its parent by sending events.

Example:

<script setup>
const emit = defineEmits(['addToCart'])

const addProduct = () => {
    emit('addToCart', {
        id: 1,
        name: 'Keyboard'
    })
}
</script>
<template>
    <button @click="addProduct">
        Add to Cart
    </button>
</template>

The parent component can listen for the event:

<ProductCard @add-to-cart="handleAddToCart" />

This creates a clean communication pattern:

  • Props: Parent to Child
  • Emits: Child to Parent

11. Understanding Lifecycle Hooks

Every Vue component has a lifecycle.

A component is created, mounted, updated, and eventually unmounted.

Vue provides lifecycle hooks that allow developers to execute code at different stages.

Some commonly used lifecycle hooks are:

HookPurposeonMountedRuns after the component is mountedonUpdatedRuns after the component updatesonUnmountedRuns after the component is unmountedonBeforeMountRuns before mountingonBeforeUnmountRuns before unmounting

Example: onMounted()

<script setup>
import { onMounted } from 'vue'

onMounted(() => {
    console.log('Component mounted successfully!')
})
</script>
<template>
    <h2>Vue Lifecycle Example</h2>
</template>

A common use case is fetching initial data when a component loads.

<script setup>
import { ref, onMounted } from 'vue'

const users = ref([])
onMounted(async () => {
    const response = await fetch('/api/users')
    users.value = await response.json()
})
</script>

In production applications, you should also handle loading states, errors, and cancellation when appropriate.

12. Understanding Vue Router

When building a multi-page frontend application, you need a way to navigate between different pages without reloading the entire application.

Vue Router is the official routing solution for Vue.js.

For example, an e-commerce application might have:

  • / — Home page
  • /products — Product listing
  • /products/1 — Product details
  • /cart — Shopping cart
  • /checkout — Checkout page

A simple route configuration looks like this:

import { createRouter, createWebHistory } from 'vue-router'

import Home from './views/Home.vue'
import Products from './views/Products.vue'
const routes = [
    {
        path: '/',
        component: Home
    },
    {
        path: '/products',
        component: Products
    }
]
const router = createRouter({
    history: createWebHistory(),
    routes
})
export default router

You can then use:

<template>
    <router-link to="/">Home</router-link>

<router-link to="/products">Products</router-link>
    <router-view />
</template>

router-link handles navigation, while router-view displays the matched component.

13. Vue.js Composition API vs Options API

Vue supports two main styles of organizing component logic.

Options API

The Options API organizes component logic into options such as data, methods, computed, and lifecycle hooks.

<script>
export default {
    data() {
        return {
            count: 0
        }
    },
methods: {
        increment() {
            this.count++
        }
    }
}
</script>
<template>
    <button @click="increment">
        {{ count }}
    </button>
</template>

Composition API

The Composition API allows developers to organize logic using functions such as ref, computed, and watch.

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
const increment = () => {
    count.value++
}
</script>
<template>
    <button @click="increment">
        {{ count }}
    </button>
</template>

Which One Should You Learn?

Both APIs are supported in Vue 3.

However, the Composition API with <script setup> is widely used in modern Vue 3 projects.

It also makes it easier to organize and reuse related logic through composables.

14. What Are Composables in Vue?

Composables are reusable functions that encapsulate reactive state and related logic.

They help developers avoid repeating the same logic across multiple components.

For example, imagine multiple components need access to the current user.

Instead of repeating the same logic everywhere, you can create a composable.

composables/useCounter.js

import { ref } from 'vue'

export function useCounter() {
    const count = ref(0)
    const increment = () => {
        count.value++
    }
    const decrement = () => {
        count.value--
    }
    return {
        count,
        increment,
        decrement
    }
}

Now use it inside a component:

<script setup>
import { useCounter } from './composables/useCounter'

const { count, increment, decrement } = useCounter()
</script>
<template>
    <h2>{{ count }}</h2>
    <button @click="increment">+</button>
    <button @click="decrement">-</button>
</template>

Composables are especially useful when building large applications with repeated frontend logic.

15. Best Practices for Vue.js Developers

Understanding Vue fundamentals is important, but writing clean and maintainable code is equally important.

Here are some practices worth following:

1. Build Reusable Components

Avoid writing your entire application inside one component.

2. Use Meaningful Component Names

Prefer ProductCard.vue instead of generic names such as Component1.vue.

3. Use Computed Properties for Derived Data

Avoid repeating complex calculations inside templates.

4. Use Stable Keys With v-for

Use unique identifiers instead of array indexes whenever possible.

5. Keep Components Focused

A component should have a clear responsibility.

6. Reuse Logic With Composables

Move reusable reactive logic into composable functions.

7. Handle API Errors Properly

Always consider loading states, validation errors, and failed requests.

8. Understand Reactivity Before Using State Libraries

Learn ref, reactive, computed, and watch before moving to more advanced state management tools.

16. What Should You Learn Next?

After understanding these fundamentals, you can gradually move toward more advanced Vue.js concepts.

Here is a suggested learning roadmap:

  1. JavaScript ES6+ fundamentals
  2. Vue 3 fundamentals
  3. Components, Props, and Emits
  4. Composition API
  5. Vue Router
  6. Pinia for state management
  7. API integration with Axios or Fetch
  8. Form validation
  9. Authentication and route protection
  10. Testing Vue components
  11. Performance optimization
  12. Building a complete project

Practice Project Ideas

Try building these projects to improve your understanding:

  • Todo Application
  • Weather Dashboard
  • Product Listing Page
  • Shopping Cart
  • Admin Dashboard
  • Inventory Management System

Building real projects will help you understand how individual Vue concepts work together.

Conclusion

Vue.js is a powerful yet approachable framework for building modern web interfaces.

Understanding its fundamentals is the first step toward becoming a better frontend developer.

Start with reactivity, directives, components, props, emits, and lifecycle hooks. Once you understand these concepts, you will find it much easier to build larger applications.

Don’t just memorize Vue syntax. Understand how data flows, how components communicate, and how reactivity works.

That’s how you move from writing Vue code to building real-world applications.

corrida_no_ar.resumo: Confira a nova medalha da São Silvestre, um influenciador banido por usar número falso na Maratona de NY, o calendário 2027 da Iguana Sports e a estreia da recordista Agnes Ngetich na maratona. Além disso, veja detalhes da Maratona de Curitiba e cupons para Uphill Corcovado…
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Sexta-feira | 13 de novembro de 2026

A medalha da 101ª edição da São Silvestre foi revelada e, na minha opinião, ficou bem bonita. O design mudou bastante em relação aos anos anteriores, que seguiam um formato muito parecido. A nova peça é redonda, com detalhes dos monumentos do percurso na frente — como o MASP e o prédio da Gazeta — e o trajeto da prova gravado no verso. Na fita, a inscrição “a primeira dos próximos cem anos” celebra o início de um novo século para a corrida.

Influenciador americano corre com número falso na Maratona de Nova York

Um influenciador americano que se gabou de ter cumprimentado a cantora Ariana Grande durante a Maratona de Nova York foi desmascarado. Após a repercussão do vídeo, descobriram que ele correu com um número de peito falsificado, que pertencia a um executivo francês. Como resultado da fraude, ele foi banido da prova por um ano. É uma situação lamentável que, infelizmente, acontece no mundo todo.

Uphill Corcovado: última chamada para o desafio no Rio

A Uphill Corcovado acontece no próximo sábado, dia 21 de novembro, no Rio de Janeiro. A prova noturna, com distâncias de 5, 10 e 21 km, oferece uma experiência única de subir o Corcovado à noite e ter uma vista incrível da cidade. Se você ainda não se inscreveu, pode usar o cupom CORRIDANOAR30 para garantir 30% de desconto.

Iguana Sports lança calendário 2027 com nova prova de 30 km

A Iguana Sports divulgou seu calendário de provas para a temporada de 2027. A principal novidade é a Ultimate SP 30K, uma nova corrida que terá percursos de 5, 10, 21.1 e 30 km. O trajeto passará por locais como o Jockey Club, Parque Villa-Lobos e USP, semelhante à segunda metade da São Paulo City Marathon. A data ainda não foi definida, mas a prova acontecerá no primeiro semestre. Além dela, o calendário inclui provas tradicionais como a Seven Run, as etapas do circuito Athenas, a Nike SP City Marathon, a Run The Bridge, a SP 10K e a Venus Women’s Half Marathon.

FlaRun: a corrida do Flamengo está de volta

A FlaRun, corrida oficial do Flamengo, está de volta e acontece no dia 29 de novembro no Aterro do Flamengo, no Rio de Janeiro. Com percursos de 3, 5 e 10 km, o evento é uma festa para a torcida rubro-negra. Para quem quiser participar, o cupom CORRIDANOAR10 dá 10% de desconto na inscrição.

Recordista mundial Agnes Ngetich fará sua estreia na maratona

Uma das estreias mais aguardadas do ano acontecerá na Maratona de Valência, em dezembro.
